t: Remove One Element to Make the Array Strictly Increasing — One-Pass Violation Repair
o: We may delete exactly one element so that what remains is strictly increasing; if the array is already strictly increasing the answer is true, since removing any single element preserves that property. In Example 1, [1,2,10,5,7] has exactly one descent, 10 > 5, and removing the 10 leaves [1,2,5,7], which is strictly increasing. In Example 2, [2,3,1,2] has the descent 3 > 1, but every possible removal still leaves a broken adjacent pair such as 2 > 1 inside [2,1,2], so the answer is false. In Example 3, [1,1,1] fails because equal neighbors violate strictness and removing one element still leaves [1,1]. With n up to 1000 even testing every single removal in O(n^2) passes, but one careful scan that repairs at most one violation achieves O(n).
k: A deletable array contains at most one descent that needs fixing: two separate descents can never be repaired by a single deletion.
When nums[i] <= nums[i-1], one of the two neighbors must go; comparing nums[i-2] with nums[i] decides locally which side to drop.
Equal neighbors are already violations because the increase must be strict, not merely non-decreasing.

a.i: Test each candidate removal directly: skip index r and verify the remaining sequence is strictly increasing. Removing the last index checks the untouched prefix, so the already-increasing case is covered automatically. This mirrors the definition perfectly and is fast enough for n <= 1000.
s: Define a check(skip) that scans nums, skipping index skip, and verifies every kept adjacent pair is strictly increasing.
Return true if check(r) holds for any r in [0, n-1].
a.t: O(n^2) — n candidate removals, each verified with a linear scan
a.sp: O(1) — the scan skips the removed index without copying the array

a.n: Approach 2: Single Pass with One Repair
a.i: Scan once and allow at most one violation. On the first descent nums[i] <= nums[i-1], either drop nums[i-1] or drop nums[i]; the choice is decidable locally. Dropping nums[i-1] is safe exactly when i == 1 or nums[i-2] < nums[i], because then its surviving neighbor relationships stay consistent. Otherwise we must drop nums[i], simulated by overwriting nums[i] with nums[i-1] so later comparisons see the retained value. Keeping the smaller predecessor whenever it is legal is never worse: any suffix that survives the stricter choice survives the lenient one too.
s: Track a boolean removed, initially false.
For each i from 1 to n-1, skip while nums[i] > nums[i-1].
On a violation, return false if removed is already true.
If i > 1 and nums[i-2] >= nums[i], set nums[i] = nums[i-1] (drop the right element); otherwise drop the left implicitly.
Return true when the scan completes.
a.t: O(n) — a single scan with constant-time handling of the one possible violation
a.sp: O(1) — one flag; the input array doubles as scratch space

w: Mention the O(n^2) definition-check first, then present the single scan as the polished answer. Pitfalls: forgetting that equality counts as a violation ([1,1,1] returns false); mishandling i == 1, where deleting the left element is always legal; and assuming the left element of a descent should always go — [2,3,1,2] forces deleting the right one. A useful invariant to state out loud: after repairing the first violation, no second violation may appear. Follow-up: allowing up to k removals reduces to checking whether the longest strictly increasing subsequence has length at least n - k.
